title: HC Seeks Clarification From BMC Over Allegation Of Favours In Road Project
excerpt: The Bombay High Court questioned the BMC over allegations of extending private benefits to commercial space by removing two public toilets.
author: Siddiqui Law Associates

content.text: The Bombay High Court recently questioned the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) over allegations of extending private benefits to commercial space by removing two public toilets situated near the Mrinal Tai Gore flyover.
The Public Interest Litigation (PIL)

A public interest litigation (PIL), filed by Vishwashanti Utkarsh Sanstha, sought directions from the Bombay High Court to restrain the BMC from demolishing the two toilets. The petition claimed that the demolition would lead to a significant public health risk, environmental hazards, and social discomfort.

The BMC had previously sent a notice on October 7, 2024, to Sulabh International Social Service, the entity responsible for maintaining the structures, to demolish the two public toilets at Cama Estate, Goregaon East. The petition alleged that this notice was issued following a request from MP Gajanan Kirtikar, who submitted that the toilets hindered road expansion crucial for easing traffic congestion.
Arguments Presented

Advocate Rahil Ahmed Siddiqui, representing Vishwashanti Utkarsh Sanstha, submitted that the toilets were built specifically to serve the local slum population and are a vital part of the government's initiative to improve sanitation in urban slums. He contended that the demolition would disproportionately affect people who cannot easily access private facilities.

Additionally, it was alleged that the actual purpose of the demolition was to subserve a private petrol pump. "The two toilets are not coming in the alignment of road widening and is only being used as an excuse by the BMC to favour the commercial industry," Siddiqui argued.

Conversely, advocates representing the BMC established that the area experiences significant traffic jams due to nearby commercial and residential developments, which compromises pedestrian safety. The BMC filed an affidavit stating that the construction of a new toilet block, located approximately 400 meters away under the Slum Sanitation Programme, is already in progress.
Court's Directives

After reviewing the submissions, a division bench led by Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Amit Borkar asserted the importance of the road widening project, noting, "Widening of roads is also very essential. We must take a step towards it even if it's coming in the way of a petrol pump."

To balance public needs, the court directed municipal authorities to find space close to the prescribed location to construct an additional permanent toilet and to install a temporary porta cabin toilet in the interim. The court has directed the BMC to file an affidavit explaining their position regarding the petitioner's objections.

title: Does BMC Favour Commercial Interests Over Public Needs? Bombay HC Raises Questions
excerpt: Vishwashanti Utkarsh Sanstha filed a public interest litigation asking the Bombay HC to order BMC to refrain from tearing down two public restrooms, citing risks to public health and the environment.
author: Siddiqui Law Associates

content.text: The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) was recently questioned by the Bombay High Court (HC) over claims that it extended private privileges to commercial property by removing two public restrooms located close to the Mrinal Tai Gore flyover.
The PIL and Public Health Concerns

Vishwashanti Utkarsh Sanstha filed a public interest litigation (PIL) requesting the Bombay HC to order the BMC to refrain from tearing down the two restrooms. The petition argued that the demolition would cause serious risks to public health, create environmental dangers, and lead to social unrest.

On October 7, 2024, the BMC had notified Sulabh International Social Service, the organization in charge of maintaining the facilities, that the two public restrooms in Cama Estate, Goregaon East, needed to be demolished. According to the petition, this notice was issued at the request of MP Gajanan Kirtikar, who claimed the structures impeded a road expansion essential for reducing local traffic.
Arguments on Behalf of Slum Dwellers

Advocate Rahil Ahmed Siddiqui, speaking on behalf of Vishwashanti Utkarsh Sanstha, argued that the restrooms were constructed specifically for local slum dwellers and are a vital component of the government's effort to enhance cleanliness in urban slums. He emphasized that those who cannot readily access private facilities would be disproportionately impacted by the demolition.

Siddiqui further asserted that the destruction was actually planned to make room for a private petrol pump, stating, "The BMC is using the two restrooms as an excuse to favour the commercial industry, and they are not coming in the alignment of road widening."
The BMC's Defense and Court's Resolution

Attorneys Chaitanya Chavan and Oorja Dhond, representing the BMC, demonstrated that the neighborhood—especially the area surrounding the petrol station—suffers from severe traffic congestion due to adjacent residential and commercial constructions, endangering pedestrian safety. Furthermore, an affidavit filed by the BMC noted that a new restroom block is currently being constructed 400 meters away under the Slum Sanitation Program.

A division bench headed by Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Amit Borkar affirmed the significance of the road widening project. To balance the competing needs, the court directed the municipal authorities to construct an additional permanent toilet nearby and install a temporary porta cabin restroom in the interim.

title: Thane Court Acquits Man In Wife's Murder Case Over Lack Of Proof
excerpt: A Thane court acquitted a 32-year-old man accused of murdering his wife in 2021, ruling that the prosecution failed to establish the foundational facts of circumstantial evidence.
author: Siddiqui Law Associates

content.text: A Thane court has acquitted a 32-year-old man accused of murdering his wife in 2021, noting that the prosecution failed to prove the "foundational facts" necessary to establish guilt in a case based on circumstantial evidence.
The Prosecution's Case

The prosecution alleged that on May 9, 2021, Shan Mohammad Shabid Ali Khan murdered his fourth wife, Arfa Khan, at their residence in Daighar in Maharashtra's Thane district. The alleged motive was Khan's suspicion that his wife was having an extramarital affair. It was claimed that he banged her head against the bathroom floor, causing fatal head injuries and facial fractures.

Neighbours reportedly found the victim lying in a pool of blood with her two-year-old child crying beside her. Following these events, Khan was charged under section 302 (murder) of the Indian Penal Code and remained in jail since June 9, 2021.
The Court's Observations on Circumstantial Evidence

While the victim's medical reports confirmed a homicidal death, Principal District and Sessions Judge SB Agrawal acquitted the accused due to the lack of a "complete and unbroken chain" connecting him to the act.

In his judgment, Judge Agrawal stated that it is incumbent on the prosecution to prove every fact forming a link in the chain of circumstances "which leads only to the hypothesis that is in consonance with guilt of the accused, ruling out any reasonable possibility of his innocence."
Failures in Evidence and Witness Testimony

The judge highlighted crucial gaps in the investigation, specifically regarding the recovery of a rolling board allegedly used in the assault. "As far as the rolling board is concerned, it is to be noted that on the very date of the incident, the spot panchanama was prepared and went on for about an hour and there is no explanation coming forward as to why blood stains on the rolling board were not found on that day," the court observed.

The court further noted that key witnesses failed to place the accused at the scene at the time of the murder. Concluding that guilt cannot be established solely on the basis of non-discharge of burden under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, the court found the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, thereby acquitting him and ordering his immediate release.

title: Thane Court Acquits Man In Wife's Murder Case Over Lack Of Proof
excerpt: A Thane court acquitted a 32-year-old man accused of murdering his fourth wife, ruling that the prosecution failed to prove foundational facts in the circumstantial case.
author: Siddiqui Law Associates

content.text: A Thane court has acquitted a 32-year-old man accused of murdering his wife in 2021, noting that the prosecution failed to prove the "foundational facts" necessary to establish guilt in a case based heavily on circumstantial evidence.
Allegations and the Motive

The prosecution alleged that on May 9, 2021, Shan Mohammad Shabid Ali Khan murdered his fourth wife, Arfa Khan, at their residence in Daighar, located in Maharashtra's Thane district. The alleged motive was the accused's suspicion that his wife was having an extramarital affair.

It was alleged that Khan banged her head against the bathroom floor, causing fatal head injuries and facial fractures. Neighbours reportedly found the victim lying in a pool of blood with her two-year-old child crying over her body. Khan was subsequently charged under Section 302 (murder) of the Indian Penal Code and had been in jail since June 9, 2021.
Burden of Proof in Circumstantial Evidence

Principal District and Sessions Judge SB Agrawal delivered the judgment, stating that it is incumbent on the prosecution to prove every fact that forms a link in the chain of circumstances. The chain must lead only to the hypothesis that aligns with the guilt of the accused, "ruling out any reasonable possibility of his innocence."

While medical reports confirmed a homicidal death, the judge noted a lack of a "complete and unbroken chain" connecting the accused to the act. The court stated, "Solely on the basis of non-discharge of burden under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, guilt cannot be brought about against the accused... it is the prosecution which has to stand on its own leg."
Evidentiary Gaps and Acquittal

The court highlighted significant gaps in the physical evidence, particularly regarding a rolling board allegedly used in the assault. The judge pointed out that despite a thorough spot panchanama conducted for an hour on the day of the incident, the blood-stained rolling board was only recovered later, without any plausible explanation for its initial absence.

Furthermore, the court observed that key witnesses did not place the accused at the scene at the time of the murder. Concluding that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the court acquitted the accused and ordered his immediate release from jail.
